title: 1.8 Million Years Ago, Early Humans Were Already Bringing Fire Into Caves
summary: Deep inside a South African cave, far beyond the reach of natural wildfires, scientists have found burned bones dating back 1.07 to 1.79 million years. The discovery at Wonderwerk Cave, published in PLOS One, provides the oldest known evidence of hominins deliberately bringing fire into a sheltered space and keeping it burning. An international team led by Dr. Liora Kolska Horwitz of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem used a novel, non-destructive technique: when exposed to specific wavelengths of light, bones that experienced intense heating produce a distinctive glow. This luminescence method, combined with chemical analyses, allowed researchers to confidently identify burned fossil bones—many from tiny rodents left by owls. Crucially, the burned remains were found in an archaeological layer associated with early Acheulean artifacts, likely linked to Homo erectus, about 30 meters inside the cave. No guano deposits were present, ruling out spontaneous combustion. The findings suggest these early humans were not yet able to create fire at will; instead, they collected it from natural sources like lightning strikes or wildfires on the savanna. Yet the repeated presence of fire indicates they actively transported and maintained it—a major behavioral milestone. Owl pellets may even have been used as fuel. "These discoveries show that early humans were not simply passive observers of natural fires," Dr. Kolska Horwitz explained. "They were actively engaging with fire and incorporating it into their lives." This pushes back the timeline of intentional fire use by hundreds of thousands of years and provides archaeologists with a powerful new tool for investigating the origins of one of humanity's most transformative technologies.
why_it_matters: Fire transformed our ancestors' survival, turning raw food into energy-dense meals that may have fueled bigger brains. Understanding exactly when and how we mastered it reveals the roots of human innovation and shows that our early relatives were far more resourceful than we once thought.

background_read: Fire control was a turning point in human evolution, allowing early ancestors to cook food (which made nutrients easier to digest and may have fueled larger brains), stay warm, and scare off predators at night.

Before this discovery, the earliest widely accepted evidence of humans using fire regularly came from a site in Israel called Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, dated to about 790,000 years ago—meaning this find may push back the timeline by hundreds of thousands of years.

Wonderwerk Cave (a huge ancient cave in South Africa with a very long record of human occupation) has yielded some of the earliest Acheulean handaxes—egg-shaped tools first made by Homo erectus, a tall, tool-using human ancestor that emerged around 2 million years ago and spread out of Africa.

Dr. Liora Kolska Horwitz (a zooarchaeologist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who studies animal bones from ancient human sites) has worked at the cave for decades, helping uncover the deep history hidden in its layers.
Fire also allowed early humans to harden wooden spears and perhaps even process medicinal plants, turning a dangerous natural force into a tool that shaped our entire way of life.

perspectives.perspective: Positive (a breakthrough in method and knowledge)
perspectives.description: The discovery gives scientists a new, non-destructive way to test for fire use at even older sites, potentially revolutionizing our knowledge of early technology. It highlights the cleverness of early hominins, who could transport and maintain fire long before they could start it themselves.

The evidence is indirect—burned bones might have been washed into the cave by floods or carried in by predators, making the claim of deliberate fire maintenance uncertain. Some archaeologists argue that true fire control only began when humans could reliably make flame, which came later.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical (placing it in human evolution)
perspectives.description: Fire use and cooking are closely tied to the brain expansion seen in Homo erectus, so this finding supports the idea that diet played a central role in our evolution. However, the timing still leaves a gap between the earliest fire caves and the anatomical changes in body and brain, which need further evidence to connect.

With luminescence techniques, researchers can now re-examine old collections from other caves across Africa and Asia for signs of fire, possibly extending the record even further back. This could reshape the story of when our ancestors moved from being passive victims of their environment to becoming active shapers of it.
